India’s Ukraine Approach Shifts From Diplomatic Advocacy to Strategic Interests: Report
evening.text:
India’s emerging peace initiative on the Russia-Ukraine conflict demonstrates a calibrated shift from diplomatic advocacy to more targeted, interest-driven engagement, according to a report.
“Rather than attempting to broker a comprehensive political settlement to a war that has repeatedly defied diplomatic intervention, New Delhi appears to be pursuing a more attainable objective: limiting the conflict’s disruptive consequences for energy security, food supplies, and maritime commerce. Conveyed during External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar’s visit to Kyiv in September, the proposal has reportedly been described by Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha as the ‘most comprehensive’ among four international initiatives, alongside those advanced by Turkey, Egypt, and the US,” former diplomat Harsh V. Pant wrote in the report in weekly current affairs and features magazine Open.
The proposal presented by India is based on three interconnected pillars – a mutual halt in attacks on energy facilities and other infrastructure, the uninterrupted movement of energy supplies and grain through the Black Sea ports, and cessation of attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea. Taken together, these measures showcase an attempt to find areas of limited convergence between Russia and Ukraine, where none of the two nations is required to make immediate concessions regarding the fundamental political and territorial questions underpinning the conflict.
India is not presenting a diplomatic formula to end the conflict but wants to establish a measure of predictability in sectors where the costs of continued hostilities affect beyond the immediate belligerents. Energy flows, food security and the safety of seafarers form practical points of engagement around which a limited understanding might be created. Reports of Russia and Ukraine’s acknowledgements of India’s efforts, along with Russian President Vladimir Putin appreciating Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s proposals and the Kremlin’s praise for New Delhi’s readiness to contribute, indicate that India retains diplomatic space with both sides.
Since the start of the conflict, India has called for dialogue and diplomacy to resolve the war. PM Modi’s statement, “this is not an era of war”, during his meeting with President Putin in Uzbekistan’s Samarkand in 2022 showcases India’s effort to preserve strategic autonomy while signalling its preference for a negotiated outcome.
“India’s more recent engagement suggests an effort to move beyond advocacy towards selective problem-solving. Jaishankar’s reported conversations with both Moscow and Kyiv on Black Sea shipping, grain and energy exports, and the possibility of reciprocal non-attack arrangements point to a more operational understanding of what Indian diplomacy might realistically achieve,” Pant wrote in the report.

evening.title: SAP's Signavio hit with function injunction in Germany
evening.text: A German court has issued an injunction banning SAP from providing certain features of its Signavio product, following a legal challenge from process mining biz Celonis. The ruling only applies to implementations in Germany, but is part of a broader legal tussle between the two companies over intellectual property. This case focuses on software which helps companies understand their own complex business processes in order to improve them and help prepare for an application migration. The Munich Regional Court ruled against SAP for infringing a Celonis patent covering the technology which determines the lead time between process stages of a process instance. The court also asked SAP to provide more information and offer financial statements about its alleged infringement. In a statement, an SAP spokesperson said: “The court’s ruling relates to one specific function within SAP Signavio Process Intelligence, not to the product as a whole. SAP Signavio Process Intelligence remains available to customers. S/4HANA Cloud migrations are not affected. SAP is working to ensure that there is no disruption to our customers.” SAP added: "SAP respectfully disagrees with the Munich court's ruling and has appealed the decision. SAP has separately challenged the validity of the asserted patent before the Federal Patent Court. In fact, the Munich court's decision represents only one of several ongoing disputes between SAP and Celonis, including patent actions brought by SAP in Germany and the United States. SAP’s first priority is ensuring that there is no disruption to our customers, and we will address all related matters through the appropriate legal channels." Celonis specializes in process mining, building software designed to gather data from people's interactions with business applications. It aims to uncover how organizations’ processes are actually performed, as opposed to how they were designed. For example, during a process mining project, pharma giant GSK discovered around 28,000 different variations for the process of running a sales order. Celonis was founded in 2011 and early customers included Siemens, with projects examining how processes run on the global engineering company’s SAP software. In 2021, SAP decided it wanted in on the same market and bought mining company Signavio, in part to help customers move from legacy software systems to the cloud. The ERP giant does not mandate Signavio for its migrations, but the software is bundled in packages under the moniker RISE with SAP, the lift-shift-and-transform commercial push SAP launched in 2021 to get users into the cloud and on its latest ERP offering, S/4HANA. The latest ruling is part of a set of legal disputes between Celonis and SAP. In March last year, Celonis filed a lawsuit in the US Court, Northern District of California, claiming the ERP giant had made it more difficult and expensive for third-party software companies to get hold of customer data stored in SAP's business software. Celonis was later allowed to amend and refile its complaint after the US court dismissed most of the claims. A trial is set for September 2027. SAP has also launched a case alleging a patent infringement action against Celonis at a Düsseldorf, Germany, court. It also filed suit in October last year at the District Court of Delaware over four US patents. Celonis has launched other cases alleging infringement by SAP, including in a Texas federal district court. ®

evening.title: Why BrahMos-2 Hangs in the Balance
evening.text:
The BrahMos-2, which was intended to be the highlight of Indo-Russian defence cooperation, has instead had a remarkably quiet development. It was widely publicised when it was announced in 2008, and by 2009 an MoU had been signed and technical specifications had been finalised; the hypersonic scramjet-powered follow-on to the BrahMos was meant to travel at speeds between Mach 7 and 8 and have a range of about 1,500 km. Now, after nearly twenty years, it has still not carried out its first flight, and it is reported that BrahMos Aerospace has put the active phase of its development on hold. The cause is not a single one but a combination of three factors: financial problems, issues concerning technology transfer, and the fact that the services establishment does not consider the price to be worthwhile.
The main figure is the price. It has been estimated that each BrahMos-2 will cost about $12.5 million, as compared with between $3 million and $4.5 million for the current BrahMos-1 series, which amounts to around Rs 40 crore per unit. That means one BrahMos-2 could cost almost the same as three BrahMos-1s. Since the weapon is intended to be fired in large numbers at hardened shelters, command centres and airbases, this kind of calculation is difficult to justify.
The other issue is the source of the speed. The BrahMos-2 has always been based on the scramjet engine, with that technology to be taken from Russia’s 3M22 Zircon, or Tsirkon, one of the most advanced hypersonic cruise missiles globally. Moscow has been unwilling to grant full transfer of the scramjet technology and is reported to be asking for a high price for the engines it does provide. This can be understood to some degree since scramjet propulsion is a top-tier capability and Russia keeps it well protected. However, for India this means that the very component which gives the missile its hypersonic performance is also the one which raises the cost and leaves the country in a position of dependence. Some reports even state that the version being offered was to be limited to Mach 6, not the Zircon’s Mach 8.
That is why the talks between India and Russia have never really got off the ground. New Delhi is looking for extensive technology sharing at a low cost, while Moscow wishes to preserve its advantage and charge for it. Even when there was excitement in 2025 about the possibility of a revival during President Putin’s visit, no agreements were reached. The position that BrahMos Aerospace has itself taken is that the BrahMos-NG meaning the lighter and smaller missile intended for the Tejas and the MiG-29—should come first, and only afterwards the hypersonic version. Because of the limited resources, the BrahMos-2 is continuing to be delayed, with flight tests now expected no earlier than 2027–28.
There is also the matter of the customer. It is said that the three services, collectively having ordered the BrahMos in large quantities, are not very enthusiastic regarding the expected per-unit cost. Their reason is practical. The BrahMos has already demonstrated its ability to penetrate layered air defences during Operation Sindoor in May 2025. While the additional advantage of a hypersonic missile is genuine it is only incremental and not sufficient to warrant a missile that would cost twice as much. Instead of pursuing a small number of very expensive hypersonic missiles which would always have a thin inventory, the services prefer to increase production of the BrahMos-1 since this would also reduce the unit cost.
That scepticism has led India to take the route of developing technologies domestically. The DRDO has been gradually improving its scramjet technology, having conducted a combustor test lasting more than 1,000 seconds in April 2025 and carrying out a trial of a full-scale, actively cooled scramjet combustor for 20 minutes at a site in Hyderabad in May 2026. As part of initiatives such as Project Vishnu, the emphasis is on hypersonic designs which are affordable so that they can be produced in large numbers, incorporating active cooling and a modular design. Once these efforts are successful, the rationale for entering into an expensive joint venture becomes even weaker, since India would then possess both the technology and the associated cost.
This does not indicate that the BrahMos-2 has been abandoned; it is still a strategic choice when it comes to certain high-value targets, and the partnership is by no means coming to an end. However, the break in activity is a clear indication of a more mature Indian strategy one that takes into account cost-per-kill and inventory depth, rather than simply relying on speed. At present, the hypersonic BrahMos remains in the planning stage, awaiting the time when both price and technology finally become viable.
EDITED BY RAUNAK KUNDE

evening.title: Admin: 'I spent all weekend on my servers' after Microsoft breaks Exchange Server with October updates
evening.text: Microsoft has acknowledged that the October 2026 Windows Server updates may be destabilizing Exchange Server. The problems are related to this list of Windows Server updates (see here) and Microsoft makes it clear they are not related to the October 2026 security updates for Exchange Server. The software giant says the bug can hit Exchange Servers running Windows Server 2016, 2019, 2022, and 2025. The glitch might not be immediate and could impact Exchange Server OWA, which can throw up connection glitches or cause lengthy email queues, "with email crawling to a halt." Rebooting the server might make the problem go away temporarily, but a more permanent workaround is a registry edit. The destabilization issue could impact Exchange Server 2016, 2019, and the new Subscription Edition (SE), says the Windows maker. Microsoft strongly advised that customers should not uninstall the October 2026 Windows Server update and stated, "Not all Exchange servers will be impacted by installation of those updates equally; the severity and speed of impact varies based on Exchange server load. Some servers might never see a problem." However, for those administrators who found their weekend swallowed by borked Exchange Servers, the registry edit is currently the only workaround. The cause of the issue is a default limit on the amount of memory used by Endpoint Mapper when handling Endpoint Lookup calls. In Microsoft's Release Health Dashboard for Windows Server 2025 (Server 2022, 2019, and 2016 are also affected), the Microsoft said: "For workloads such as Exchange Server, the default limit of 512 simultaneous Endpoint Lookup calls might not be sufficient under heavy load." Hence, the instruction to use a registry setting to increase the maximum. It added, "We are investigating this issue and will provide more information when it is available." Customers were understandably frustrated. On Microsoft's support page, one wrote, "We have had the problem like every 20h since Wednesday, when we installed the windows updates for October and the exchange su. Reboot only solution," before noting that the registry setting appeared to have improved things. Another fumed, "Also please release your updates tested and without problems. Without giving us the job to test for you. We're already paying for the software and you want to make tests with us?! I spent all weekend on my servers because of this." The issue is bad form on the part of Microsoft and appears to be the result of a poorly thought-through default applied in the operating system which impacted Exchange Server. Microsoft has yet to commit to issuing an out-of-band update to resolve the issue, after all, not every customer is affected, and the problem depends heavily on how busy a server is. However, at least there's a registry workaround that might do the trick while Microsoft ponders its next move. ®

evening.text:
At least 15 houses belonging to the Kuki tribal community were reportedly burnt by suspected militants in Chassad village in Manipur’s Kamjong district, forcing civilians to flee their homes and take shelter in nearby forest areas and a camp of security forces, officials and local sources said on Sunday.
The incident occurred late on Saturday night, following a gun attack in the village earlier in the day in which a Kuki civilian, identified as Seikhohao Haokip, was killed and four others sustained bullet injuries, according to reports.
Deputy Chief Minister Nemcha Kipgen condemned the violence, expressing grief over Haokip’s death and concern for the injured village leaders and displaced families. Describing the burning of houses as an intolerable crime, Kipgen said she had directed the district administration, state police and security forces to maintain round-the-clock vigilance, protect civilians and their property, and ensure that those responsible for the violence were brought to justice.
A police official said that a joint column of the Assam Rifles, the Border Security Force (BSF) and Kamjong Police had been deployed in the affected area to bring the situation under control.
In a separate incident at Kamjong district headquarters on Saturday night, three Tangkhul Naga civilians sustained bullet injuries in an attack reportedly involving rival armed groups. The injured were identified as T. Chithung, S. Malung and M. Shithung. They were admitted to Kamjong Hospital, where their condition was reported to be stable.
Both Chassad village and Kamjong district headquarters are located near the India-Myanmar border, a sensitive area that has witnessed security concerns amid tensions between armed groups.
According to local accounts, residents fled their homes amid fears for their safety. Chassad Police Station reportedly received information about the incident on Sunday. A spot inquiry had not been conducted by the time of reporting, reportedly due to a shortage of personnel. The full extent of the damage caused by the arson, the circumstances surrounding the attacks and the identities of those involved remain unverified.
The Kuki-Zo Council (KZC), the apex body of the Kuki-Zo tribals, in a statement said that the security situation in Kamjong district, particularly Chassad village, has deteriorated alarmingly. Within just over a week, four Kuki-Zo civilians have been killed, exposing the government’s failure to protect innocent lives, the organisation said.
The KZC questioned why NSCN-IM cadres are reportedly allowed to operate freely in Kamjong, Ukhrul and Chandel districts, despite the ceasefire arrangement being understood to apply to Nagaland. “The Government of India must clarify this situation and take immediate action to stop further attacks. An economic embargo is also reportedly preventing Kuki-Zo civilians in Kamjong from purchasing essential commodities,” the KZC said.
The tribal body demanded unrestricted access to essential supplies and the immediate deployment of Central security forces between the Police Station and Chassad village to protect civilians. KZC urged both the governments of India and Manipur to ensure civilian protection, hold those responsible accountable, provide ex-gratia assistance to the bereaved families, and compensate those whose houses have been burnt.
The Kuki-Zo people are citizens of India and are entitled to equal protection under the Constitution. The government must act urgently to prevent further loss of life and ensure their safety and dignity, the statement said.

evening.title: Microsoft abandons UK AI supercomputer as grid struggles to keep up
evening.text: Microsoft has reportedly pulled out of plans for Britain's largest AI supercomputer, because the government-backed project is facing the rather inconvenient problem of having no electricity to run it. The tech giant has terminated its agreement with British AI infrastructure startup Nscale for a planned datacenter in Loughton, Essex, according to The Telegraph, which first reported the withdrawal on Sunday. The decision follows reports that the site, which was supposed to begin operating in 2027, might not receive enough electricity from the grid until the early to mid-2030s. Microsoft was expected to be the anchor customer at Loughton, which Nscale had pitched as the UK's largest sovereign AI datacenter. Its departure leaves Nscale without a publicly announced customer for the site, although the neocloud insists the project is still going ahead. When the deal was announced in September 2025, the plan was to pack 23,040 Nvidia GB300 GPUs into a 50MW facility, with room to expand to 90MW. Microsoft would use the computing power for its Azure cloud services, with the first chips expected in early 2027. One important detail remained: how to power it. As The Guardian reported last month, UK Power Networks warned Nscale that the grid capacity needed might not be available until the 2030s. A UK Power Networks spokesperson told The Register it could not discuss individual connections due to obligations under Section 105 of the Utilities Act. "However, in general, many datacenters, whilst they can connect to our distribution network, are awaiting works on the national transmission network which we do not own," the spokesperson said. Nscale, meanwhile, isn't letting the small matter of losing its biggest customer dampen its enthusiasm. “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK. Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts,” Nscale told The Register. Microsoft did not respond to a request for comment. The project has already had its share of awkward moments. In March, it was revealed that the site earmarked for Britain's AI supercomputer was still being used as a scaffolding yard. Nscale has since cleared the land, but removing the scaffolding has proved easier than securing electricity. The government might be feeling a little red-faced too, having trumpeted the Loughton project as part of Microsoft's £22 billion UK investment announcement in September 2025. Just over a year later, Microsoft has walked away, and the site is still facing years of delays in getting the power it needs. The grid problems extend well beyond Essex. Ofgem proposed charging datacenter developers for connection requests earlier this year, hoping to discourage speculative projects from clogging up the queue. Demand for new connections had surged from 41GW to 125GW in less than a year, with datacenters accounting for at least 80GW. Some UK datacenter developers have turned to gas-powered generation rather than wait years for a grid connection, while others face growing resistance from the people living nearby. Residents near Google's Waltham Cross facility complained about noise, lighting and poor consultation at a public meeting in July. Britain isn’t alone in finding that the AI boom comes with substantial infrastructure demands. In the US, public enthusiasm for datacenters appears to be cooling, with concerns about electricity costs and environmental impacts increasingly souring attitudes towards new developments. For all the billions being thrown at AI infrastructure, the industry is discovering that building datacenters is the easy part. Getting them connected to the grid, and keeping the neighbors happy, is proving rather more difficult. ®

evening.text:
A fighter aircraft captured on camera against the clouds over Goa has been speculated to be a Rafale M, the carrier variant chosen for the Indian Navy. The picture was posted on social media by Admiral Arun Prakash (Retd), former Chief of Naval Staff, and seems to depict a Rafale-family aircraft, but its identity and the circumstances of the flight have not been confirmed.
The sighting has led to questions as to whether a French naval Rafale could be in India for testing or evaluation for purposes of the Indian Navy’s planned induction of the aircraft. However, the aircraft’s identity, operator and purpose of the flight have not been officially confirmed.
The Indian Navy signed an agreement with France on 28 April 2025 to acquire 26 Rafale Marine fighters, including 22 single-seat aircraft and four twin-seat trainers. The contract includes training, simulators, weapons, associated equipment and performance-based logistics. The Ministry of Defence has stated that the delivery of the aircraft will be completed by 2030.
Goa is a natural location for the testing of naval fighters, due to the Indian Navy’s Shore Based Test Facility at INS Hansa, near Dabolim. The facility has previously been used to test carrier-capable aircraft in conditions simulating those of an aircraft carrier. The Rafale M was tested there in India’s previous fighter evaluation process, before the Navy selected it for its future carrier-based combat fleet.
The Rafale M differs in a number of significant respects to the land-based Rafale operated by the Indian Air Force. It has a reinforced landing structure and arrestor hook for carrier recovery, along with other modifications required for operations from an aircraft carrier. The launch bar seen on a naval fighter is another distinguishing feature, although the photograph is not sufficient to confirm the identity or ownership of the aircraft.If the aircraft photographed above Goa is indeed a Rafale M, then there are several possibilities as to what it could be doing there. It could be associated with French testing activity, a demonstration or other flight connected with naval aviation. A link to the preparation for the Indian Navy’s future fleet is plausible, but there is currently no official evidence to establish such a purpose.
For now, the Goa photograph is an intriguing sighting rather than an indication of the arrival of an Indian Navy Rafale M for trials. Confirmation from the Indian Navy, the French Navy or Dassault Aviation would be required to establish the aircraft’s identity and whether its flight was connected with India’s procurement programme.

evening.title: DRDO’s Blueprint, Private Sector’s Build: Why India Needs a Second Design Track
evening.text:
There is a persistent bottleneck in India’s defence-industrial model that rarely gets discussed with the bluntness it deserves: DRDO remains for almost every major weapons system the sole design authority, and everything downstream of that single point of design failure inherits that bottleneck’s fragility. A single DRDO laboratory simultaneously responsible for original design, prototype validation, and every subsequent variant or upgrade of a system, limits the institute’s limited engineering bandwidth to a ceiling on how fast the entire programme, and every downstream private-sector manufacturing partner, can move.
The fix is not to strip DRDO of its design authority, which remains genuinely essential for baseline research, classified technology development, and systems where national security considerations demand tight government control. The fix is to formally create a second design track, where private-sector engineering houses are licensed to take a DRDO baseline design and develop parallel variants, upgrades and derivative products under a structured technology-transfer and design-rights framework, without needing to route every incremental change back through the originating DRDO lab.
This is not a foreign concept to Indian industry. Tata Advanced Systems, Larsen & Toubro’s defence engineering arm, Bharat Forge’s Kalyani Strategic Systems, and Adani Defence have all built genuine systems-engineering depth over the previous decade, moving well beyond the licensed-manufacturing roles Indian private defence firms were largely confined to a generation ago. What they mostly lack is not capability but authorised access — the formal design_rights and technical-data packages that would let them independently develop, say, a lighter export variant of an Akash battery, or a ruggedised desert-configuration derivative of a DRDO-designed vehicle, without every drawing change requiring DRDO sign-off from the original design team.
Israel’s model offers a useful comparison. IAI, Rafael, and Elbit operate with far more design autonomy relative to Israel’s Ministry of Defence research establishment than Indian private firms currently have relative to DRDO, and that autonomy is precisely why Israeli defence firms can iterate export variants and rapid upgrades at a pace that consistently outstrips comparable Indian programmes. The Israeli government retains oversight and export-control authority, but it does not insist on being the sole design bottleneck for every derivative product built on a baseline government-funded technology.
Building this second track in India requires three concrete institutional moves. First, a formal technology-data-package licensing framework that transfers genuine design rights, not merely manufacturing drawings, to qualified private partners for defined derivative work. Second, liability and certification protocols that let private-sector-designed variants receive independent airworthiness or ordnance-safety certification without needing the originating DRDO lab to personally validate every change, so long as the private partner meets defined engineering and testing standards. Third, a revenue-sharing or royalty structure that gives DRDO labs a continuing financial stake in derivative products built on their baseline designs, so that opening up design access is not perceived internally as a loss of institutional relevance or funding.
None of this diminishes DRDO’s role as India’s primary defence research institution. It multiplies DRDO’s effective engineering output by letting private-sector partners absorb derivative and variant-development work that currently competes for the same limited lab bandwidth as frontier research. A defence-industrial base with one design authority for every major platform will always move at the speed of that authority’s weakest bottleneck. A defence-industrial base with a genuine second design track, properly licensed and properly incentivised, can move at the speed of its fastest capable partner instead.

Broadcom Wi-Fi bug turns sweet 16, still lets strangers hijack your router
evening.text: A 16-year-old security flaw in Broadcom's Wi-Fi software could let attackers hijack millions of routers without knowing the network password, even though the chipmaker reportedly knew about the problem since 2018. Security researcher Quentin Kaiser disclosed the vulnerability, dubbed "WPSplinter," revealing two bugs in Broadcom's proprietary Wi-Fi implementation that date back to at least 2010. An attempted fix arrived eight years later, but Kaiser claims it didn't fully resolve the problem. The bugs lie in Broadcom's handling of Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS), the feature that lets users connect devices to a wireless network without manually entering a password. Kaiser found that specially crafted WPS messages could corrupt the router's memory, allowing someone within Wi-Fi range to run their own code on the device. They wouldn't need the Wi-Fi password, and the router's owner wouldn't have to do a thing. Kaiser demonstrated working exploits against routers supplied by Belgian internet providers Proximus and Orange. In one attack against an ASKEY TCG3000 gateway, he ran code on the device, pulled its Wi-Fi password from memory, and sent it back over the air. He then used the stolen credentials to join the network. He also found the flaw in Netgear and Technicolor routers supplied by VOO. He estimates that around 850,000 Proximus gateways could be affected, along with 500,000 at VOO and 210,000 at Orange Belgium. That puts the potential total at 1.56 million routers in Belgium alone, although Kaiser admits the figures are rough estimates. However, the problem is unlikely to stop at the Belgian border. Broadcom's Wi-Fi technology is used by dozens of manufacturers across hundreds of products, meaning the number of affected devices worldwide could be considerably higher. According to Kaiser, the chipmaker knew about the vulnerability back in 2018 and released a partial fix without publicly disclosing the problem. It subsequently recommended that manufacturers move away from its proprietary implementation and use the open-source hostapd software instead. Owners of routers running Broadcom's older eCos-based chips, including the BCM3380, BCM3383, and BCM33834, are in a particularly grim position. Kaiser calls the flaw a "forever day," meaning those devices may never get a fix. Routers using Linux-based BCM3390, BCM65xx, and BCM68xx chips aren't necessarily off the hook either, unless their manufacturers switch to hostapd. That leaves some older routers with no obvious route to a fix, while others depend on their manufacturers updating software that may be years out of support. Kaiser first reported the vulnerabilities to Broadcom on July 18, followed by a second report on July 27, giving the company and affected vendors 90 days before public disclosure. Broadcom responded on July 28 to say a patch was available and advised him to contact affected manufacturers directly. The following day, however, the company declined to assign a CVE identifier or provide him with a copy of the notification it said it had sent to manufacturers through its customer portal. Kaiser also contacted Proximus, attempted to reach Orange Belgium and VOO, and passed his findings to Belgium's national cybersecurity authorities. He subsequently opened a case with CERT/CC, which closed it on August 4 because Broadcom was itself a CVE Numbering Authority and had declined to register the vulnerability. By October 15, a day before his presentation, Kaiser said none of the affected devices he had identified had received a patch. Kaiser hasn't reported evidence of attacks in the wild, but the potential for mischief is considerable. Someone parked outside a home or office could potentially compromise a vulnerable router, steal network credentials, or use their access to interfere with traffic. Kaiser also credited AI with speeding up the investigation. He reckons the work would ordinarily have taken him months, but with the help of frontier models, he finished it in less than a week. ®

evening.text:
Nearly 100 years after the dirigible Graf Zeppelin made the first nonstop airship journey across the Pacific Ocean, another airship has successfully completed a round-trip flight from New Mexico to Japan and back. But the significance of this modern feat was less about the journey's length and more about its purpose: demonstrating how a lighter-than-air platform can act as a cell phone tower in the sky.

The trans-Pacific flight that took place over a month between August and September 2026 was the most notable milestone yet for Sceye, a US aerospace company based near Albuquerque, New Mexico. Sceye has developed an uncrewed platform filled with helium for buoyancy and equipped with an electric-powered propeller for active propulsion, allowing it to resist most strong winds and keep hovering over the same location for long periods. The platform also uses top-mounted solar panels and onboard batteries to stay powered for stratospheric operations around the clock.

“We can stay over an area of operation, and we do that in the stratosphere right around 60,000 feet, so we're twice as high as air traffic and we're above the jet stream, and yet 30 times closer than low-Earth orbit satellites,” Mikkel Frandsen, founder and CEO of Sceye, told Ars. “We can fly through day and night until the sun comes up the next morning and recharges the batteries, at which point we're still at the same altitude and still over the same area of operation.”

evening.text: It's been nearly half a century since the Voyager probes launched from Earth on a mission to explore the outer solar system, and they're still running. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle on this page, Spotify, Apple Podcasts, or YouTube. You can also subscribe on those platforms to be notified when a new episode goes live. You're probably familiar with some of Voyager's iconic images, like the Pale Blue Dot and and its portraits of the outer planets. Those photos and observations wouldn't have been possible without Voyager's imaging team, eight members of which were selected from scientists from around the world. The UK's sole representative, Dr. Garry Hunt, joins us on this episode of The Kettle to discuss his role in the Voyager program, the future of the mission, and the state of science in the UK, US, and beyond. A lightly edited transcript is included below: Brandon (00:01) Hi everyone, and welcome to another episode of The Register’s Kettle Podcast. I'm your host, Brandon Vigliarolo, and we have a very special episode for you this week. We're gonna step away from the doom and gloom of AI and the silliness of Silicon Valley to talk about something and to someone of considerably more historic importance. The Voyager space missions will mark fifty years of exploring the solar system and beyond next year. With us to talk about this is Reg Reporter Richard Speed and our very special guest, British astrophysicist Dr. Gary Hunt who was a member of the original Voyager imaging team. Thank you so much, Dr. Hunt, for coming on. And I'm gonna turn this over to Richard today, since you two have such a history together working on stories for The Reg, and I'm excited to hear about what he's going to pick your brain about. So Richard, take it away. Richard Speed (00:46) Well Dr. Hunt, we've spoken a lot about the Voyager project over the years, but for anyone who's not aware of it, I wonder if you could summarize the mission, which is, I know, a big ask, and also what your role in it is and was. Garry Hunt (01:00) Well indeed, it's a unique mission in the sense that every 176 years the major planets Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, line up virtually in a straight line. And we wanted to explore the outer planets 'cause we've never been there before. I'm talking in the 1970s, late 1960s, '70s. So this is an unknown world. We thought that the major planets were keys to understanding the origin of the solar system, indeed the origin of life, so sending space missions there was a priority. But it needed to be done in a very economical way. With the planets lined up, that meant we could get there in the quickest way, requiring less fuel, and it would be the best way of going about it. So the opportunity came and NASA funded a mission to send two spacecraft at this unique time, which was in the mid '70s, 1977, to the major planets. NASA sent out an invitation to tender. They selected the ten instruments. Imaging had as an instrument in concept had been suggested, but they wanted a team of real scientists, not astronomers, not basic astronomers. They understood this is a chance to do real detailed science, real physics, real chemistry, the whole understanding of what went on. So they were looking for an interdisciplinary group of people. They selected eight people from invitations and I gather there were about nearly a thousand people proposed and of those eight I was chosen. Brandon (02:43) Wow. Garry Hunt (02:44) So I decided I suddenly found myself in this incredible position. I'm there to represent atmospheric physics. I want to understand the physics, the meteorology of the major planets. So here is an opportunity to explore the outer planets to learn about why we wanted to go to Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. However, funding was tight. The president at the time was Nixon, and we only had funding as far as Jupiter and Saturn. So we were treading new territory. At the time the mission was sort of decided, we had not been through the asteroid belt. So the first question was: would the spacecraft even get that far? And of course the pioneers had just been launched at the beginning of the '70s and they managed to get through and raised a lot of questions. So I was part of the imaging team, this amazing set of what I will call prima donnas, because we all were. They were from Carl Sagan to Vern Suomi, who was a meteorologist, to Brad Smith, a whole collection of people. And we had to design the imaging system, the cameras, and be part of the organization that developed the choice of trajectories and all the other facets of this mission. In other words, we had to understand the risks as well as the potential rewards that came from it. So it was a big responsibility. And to put the whole thing in real context, I learnt in December '72 from NASA that I'd been selected. We had our first mission meetings in February of '73, and we had until the summer of 1977 to get the spacecraft launched. And the window for launching was ten days. So this was really a big precision job. So large responsibility and had many opportunities, not only to do the science, but the work that I was doing when I took the data back to the UK was to actually serve as a trigger for planetary research within the UK. So this really was a major major part of a new world, new understanding. And as we have learned over the years, we have made history and just about all the observations we've made. Richard Speed (05:16) Okay, great, thank you. So, I mean, as you said, it's been coming out for half a century, 50 years since the spacecraft were launched on their mission and they've been, as you say, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, and so on. I was just wondering, why do you think they've lasted for so long? Because it's just incredible, really if you think about it. Garry Hunt (05:36) Well, firstly I will put my hand up and say that the engineers of JPL are exceptional. We've had a few hitches and they've overcome it. First of all, we also said we want a spacecraft. It's going to unknown territories. We don't know how long it's going to last. Reliability was the key. So it was built around the mariners, which have been the bedrock of the earlier missions to around Mars and flying by Venus. So that was the first thing. And so many of the aspects of it were built from equipment from the mid-sixties. So the issue is even more exciting to think that here we are 50 years after launch flying a spacecraft with equipment which was already 10 years old by the time we got it there. So this really is an example of reliability, which is the bottleneck. And of course, the other aspect of it we built in redundancy as well. So we knew that, if things went wrong, we had to find a way of easily overcoming it. As it's drifting away at the speed of thirty thousand miles an hour, you can't just sort of go out and repair it. You've got to be able to do things while the spacecraft is in motion. So there's a certain amount of redundancy, built in reliability, incredibly good careful planning, absolutely brilliant engineers who to this day are doing the most incredible things. Richard Speed (07:05) Well, yes, I have to say, I agree, having spoken to the current Voyager team, they are a bunch of very impressive individuals. Brandon (09:00) I really hope that's not the case. Personally I hope that there's some development in deep space monitoring over the next few years that would enable us to keep picking it up beyond that. Or do you think it's simply a matter of distance and background noise that it would be unreachable? Garry Hunt (09:10) The signal is incredibly weak. and there'd be insufficient power in the spacecraft to actually power it. They've got to have some form of heating. It's pretty cold out there. or virtually everything has been turned off. They've just done a major activity with the onboard power system. They literally have done everything they can. We reckon to 2035 we will still be able – that'll be about the time it'll be too weak for anything on Earth to be able to pick it up. So that literally is the time we were anticipating the end would come, if we can keep the politicians out of the way. Richard Speed (09:51) Well, absolutely and I mean I I think as we spoke recently it's approaching a one light day to kind of get a feeling of how far away these things are now where it takes an entire day to send a command to spacecraft a light day for the command to come back. Garry Hunt (10:06) Well, I think the issue is it's one light day in distance. Now if I'm sending you a message, suppose I'm speaking to you and you're on Voyager. This is the furthest anything it has ever got that we've been able to record. Voyager 2 will not get there until about 2030, I think it is. Because it's on a different path. But these are immense distances. So it's never happened before. It actually occurs, if you want UK time, on the 18th of November at 10.06 in the morning [0206 Pacific Time, 0506 EST]. So look at your watch when that time comes up and say, that's where Voyager 1 is. Richard Speed (11:00) I must admit, speaking to the JPL team, and again, we work in technology, the thought of the fact you would send a command to the spacecraft, you won't even know if it's worked until the following day or a day or so later, at which point it could have done something awful to the spacecraft and it's too late to fix it. I just can't get my head around that kind of risk analysis and risk assessment, which you must do. Garry Hunt (11:23) Well, we've we've had that situation occur because you probably remember several months ago, they wasn't replying to signals and they discovered that the dish was actually pointing slightly away so it could not be picked up in Goldstone, but managed to find a way of turning it around so it could actually recommunicate. And one of the things I find quite incredible, every book I pick up with the solar system and the planets, it comes to the Voyager observations, we made history. This is almost like the Bayou tapestry, I guess, of a planetary exploration. Brandon (14:11) Mm-hmm. Richard Speed (14:16) Absolutely, it's very exciting. It must have been very exciting that almost every day, month or year there was a new discovery, something which no one else had seen before you. Garry Hunt (14:27) Well I gather they are, because we had eighty thousand images and if you do a count of the number of satellites now, we only had a few ten or so around Saturn at the time of Voyager's launch. We're now in the hundreds. So the objects are still being found. So it was a mission of trade-offs, it was a mission of using incredible talent, but one of the most important things that came out of Voyager was this doing what we're doing now, sharing the results. We had terrifically good press conferences every morning. We met regularly with the press and we did television, all regularly, just so people kept up to date. I always thought that the taxpayer who had paid for this mission and it cost 800 million dollars, well eight cents per American per year, which is pretty good in value for money. We should share the results with them. And to this day I go around giving talks to people, people ask me fundamental questions and I'm delighted to be able to share the results with them. Richard Speed (16:37) That's great. Brandon (16:38) Yeah. Richard Speed (16:39) Now looking at the current situation, NASA and the US space program in general, I know obviously you've been out of that for quite some time, but it seems to be much more focused on the commercial sector these days. It's commercial providers, commercial vendors. mean, one, do you think something like Voyager would even be possible now, would even be a thing that NASA would attempt? And what do you make of the impact that commercial vendors are having? Garry Hunt (17:01) Well, the commercial world has changed it dramatically. We've gone from exploration to exploitation. And also the way in which money is spent by governments has changed from doing scientific analysis and really deep exploratory activities to saying, okay, we've got to focus on defence, we've got to focus on other elements to do with the economies. And most nations' economies are struggling. So science spending is a bit of a delicate issue at the present time. So the commercial side wants return. If I'm in, and NASA's budget is being cut back, and therefore money for space activities has got to come from people with deep pockets, investors. And now if you're an investor, you'll want a return on your money quickly and have some idea of a reliable expectation. Would you invest on a mission where you wouldn't get your return for fifty years? I doubt it. So it will be some form of science exploration with a small amount of funding. Would you get a mission like Voyager again? Well, I hope so, but things have got to improve. We've got to have better power systems, we've got to have a whole variety of ways of doing things differently. But take it in mind, we're talking here about a mission launched fifty years ago, which went to Uranus and Neptune, over forty years ago. Nothing else has been there since. If you've had a glimpse of these objects once, that was one snapshot. Is that a real indication of what takes place? Have we seen things properly? Yes, we're getting good pictures from the James Webb telescope and they're giving us a new picture of it, but that's not enough. So we've got to have missions out there, but they won't necessarily come from the US or indeed Europe, they could well come from China. Which has already publicly said: we're planning to go to Uranus. So who knows what's going to do it. But the balance between commercial and science has changed dramatically. Yeah, there wasn't much commercial work in the past. And the scientific side depends on the way governments fund it. And to be absolutely honest, at the present time it's pretty appalling. Richard Speed (19:28) What do you guys think? Brandon (19:28) Yeah, and it even makes me think about how the Voyager mission felt like an expectation to the taxpayers, right? You need to share this information. The nation has paid for it. And I feel like maybe even if there was good science being done, it might not be as publicly discussed or as much of a sort of national thing if it's being part of a private industry that expects personal returns. Garry Hunt (19:47) I think that's a very good point because the average person is really interested. Look how much science really gets covered in the media. Very little. And this is one of the sad things, but there is so much we've got still got to learn. And we've got to be inquisitive. That is how the human race has made progress and to cut it off and to take away these opportunities is crazy. Look about going to Mars and Mars sample return. Lying on Mars at the moment are all the rocks that America has so delicately collected, ready to be picked up by a future mission, which NASA is not funding. So the Chinese will not likely pick it up, bring it back and say, We've got these, we think they're yours, we'll analyze them for you. That could well happen. Richard Speed (20:44) I mean funding is a very important question, particularly around science. I mean looking closer to home and the UK, I mean and also the US perhaps, what do you make of the status of science in this nation, in these nations to date versus the perception maybe 30, 40 years ago? Garry Hunt (21:02) I think it's pretty terrible, to be absolutely honest. I think that some shocking mistakes have been made. We had stuck our toes in the water and set up a space agency. So what do we do? We were the UK government, they sucked it into a government department, which I immediately said, and so did everybody else, that's a barmy thing to do. Because you know that you've you've actually immediately said by sucking it into a government department, it's at the mercy of the way they juggle around with government and if they close down or reshape a government department, that could disappear, or its funding could be drastically rerouted. And that's exactly what's happening. We have no real control over it. So I think science, quite honestly, in this country and indeed in the United States is not being funded properly. The kickback in the US is pretty serious because as soon as people start drifting away from science, industry starts drifting away from science. And the way your research, your PhDs are funded, it has a big industrial component and that's being affected. So for a world which is highly technical, we are not focusing and not using it and not developing it in a way that I think is appropriate. Richard Speed (22:22) In the 1970s, there was, I read about concerns about a brain drain from the UK to other countries like the US. I mean, do you think that's kind of reversed now in that we're seeing a brain drain going the other direction? Instead of going to the US, it's now Europe or further east that is attracting all the skills and brains, really. Garry Hunt (22:41) Well I think it is a very interesting question. I actually did 'brain drain,' you know, I just plucked out of Oxford and went to California. And the UK is you know, when you've got universities giving up physics departments, cutting back on major projects, cutting about the science program, what's the attraction? So the question is what is science in the future? And it's not the sort of science in a way that my career necessarily developed, It is changed because of the more automated technical ways of operating. For Europe, and if you take ESA, which has got terrific ideas, but its budget depends on what each country can provide as their contribution. And the issue we have to put our eyes on and think about very carefully is: defence is a major component we've all got to think about. We're talking about space and how space is being developed. We talked about commercial, we we talked about scientific research, but we didn't talk about scientific defence. And it's the defence side where the largest slab of money will be going in the future. Where already, UK satellites have been affected by Russian satellites. The Russians and the Chinese already have the ability to shoot down satellites in orbit. The Chinese are the only ones able to refuel in orbit. So there are a lot of very, very serious issues to do with defence and we've got to worry a great deal about a rogue satellite getting up there. Richard Speed (24:30) Well, yes, I mean, you mentioned defense. Obviously, in recent weeks, there was confirmation of what we've long suspected, which is that the US confirmed that it had, I don't know if one would say weapons in orbit, that they have, you know, aggressive satellites in orbit. Yeah. Brandon (24:45) Mm-hmm. Yeah, they were pretty non specific. Yeah. Garry Hunt (24:44) And I think it is in that we can go one stage further and say we've talked about going to the Moon and such like, all of which is pretty debatable and raises questions. But already people are talking about l let's put a nuclear power station up into space, we can, you know, use that as part of our space structure in orbit. Let's put a nuclear power plant on the moon. You think of the defence implications of what that actually means. Very simple. Well yeah well the other the other point about about all the debris up there as well, as soon as Hollywood gets up there and starts making a film, this problem is serious. Richard Speed (25:19) Well, I've seen Space 1999. I know how that all ends. Brandon (25:24) Yeah. Richard Speed (25:34) Well, Dr. Hunt, I guess finally, on hopefully a more positive note, but I'm not so sure now, what advice would, based on your experiences, would you give to a person who was considering a career in science, in space exploration? It doesn't have the same, perhaps cachet it might have had 40, 50 years ago, but one, do you think it's a worthwhile career for a person to pursue? I mean, we need that pipeline of people. Garry Hunt (25:59) That's a very good question. And the first thing I would say is I never had a career, went into space. That wasn't my intention. I will give you that I read mathematics for my first degree. I did mathematical physics. I then had a fellowship at Oxford, which linked me between a computer research lab in Harwell and took my skills from there into working in atmospheric physics in Oxford and went that way. So it says what you'd be studying, the subjects you've got to have. And I put a big red line underneath it. You've got to be good at mathematics, without question. You've got to be good at computer science, and you've got to have a good basis in physics. They're the three things you're going to have. But what you're also going to see, and what's also fundamental, is a dramatic change in our university structures. America already has a hugely imaginative way of going about its education. Arizona State and MIT are already using AI to restructure. Why are we still teaching in silos when the work that we're talking about and any form of space exploration or otherwise is interdisciplinary? So in developing your career, shall we say, or at least having the skills to be able to be employed in it, and space can be anything between a lawyer, a medic, as well as a scientist. A whole range of disciplines are in there now. You've got a much broader approach to be involved in that type of program. But you've got to be good at maths, you've got to be good at computer science, and you've got to have a good understanding of physics. Richard Speed (27:45) There we go. Well, thank you very much. Dr. Hunt. Brandon (27:48) Yeah, thank you so much for coming on. Garry Hunt (27:57) Thank you very much. Brandon (27:58) I really appreciate having a chance to talk with someone who is so, you know, important in the history of of the outer space exploration of the outer solar system. It's really fantastic, to have the chance to chat and to share it with our listeners. And to share it with our listeners at The Register. We really hope you enjoyed this special episode. And, you know, hopefully next time we have Dr. Hunt on, we can have some more optimistic news to share about the future of the space program and science. So be sure to tune in on a future episode of the Kettle to hear all about it. ®

evening.title: Museum exhibit reveals the intricate workings of a knackered Dell
evening.text: Today's entry in the catalog of bork comes from Coventry's Herbert Art Gallery & Museum, where an information terminal is showing more about the hardware behind the scenes than the objects on display. Register reader Jeffrey Borinsky spotted the panel, which should have demonstrated a Jacquard loom in action but was instead displaying a warning about its host PC's failing battery. The Jacquard loom was a clever device dating back to the dawn of the 19th century. It used punched cards to control a loom's weaving patterns. The result was complicated and repeatable textile designs that reduced the need for skilled humans. Register readers of a certain age are doubtless nodding sagely at the mention of punched cards, which would go on to become foundational in the world of computing. Borinsky reported that several screens at the museum were in distress. Ribbon weaving was Coventry's main industry from the early 1700s until the 1860s, so a demonstration of Jacquard weaving fits right in, even if the bleating about the BIOS battery was probably not what Joseph Jacquard had in mind. The device running behind the scenes is a Dell OptiPlex 755, likely from around 2007. Not quite centuries old like a Jacquard loom, but certainly getting on a bit in the IT world. The first iPhone arrived in 2007, and a PC of a similar vintage likely shipped with Windows XP or Windows Vista. The CMOS battery is on the way out. Dell specifies a CR2032 coin cell, so replacement should be straightforward after disconnecting the power and taking anti-static precautions. Rather less traumatic than the head-in-hands moment when a retro enthusiast discovers a leaking battery has eaten through delicate circuit traces. A fresh battery and restored BIOS settings should be enough to get the loom demonstration weaving again. Given how important punched cards became in the history of computing, we'd recommend visiting anywhere that shows how a Jacquard loom operated. At least it didn't need a battery-backed BIOS to do its thing. ®
